abstract.t: RFC 8693 defines the act claim for multi-hop actor identification in JWTs but does not record per-hop authorization constraints or provide delegator cryptographic confirmation. This specification defines the delegation_chain JWT claim as a structured companion to act: an ordered array of delegation records capturing the Authorization Server's attestation, the authorization constraints delegated at each hop (expressed as scope, with an opaque reference for deployments that use structured authorization constraints), and an optional delegator cryptographic confirmation. act and delegation_chain together provide runtime authorization and verifiable delegation lineage. The specification defines the validation rules a Resource Server applies to the chain, the Token Exchange flow through which chains are extended, and how a chain survives delegation across trust domain boundaries. For multi-hop chains, each record carries a prev_record_hash value that cryptographically binds the chain's ordering, and the specification states explicitly which ordering guarantees this mechanism does and does not provide.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: In multi-agent systems, a primary agent (Agent A) may need to delegate a subset of its authorized operations to a secondary agent (Agent B), which may in turn delegate further to Agent C. Each delegation hop must preserve the original user's authorization intent while constraining what each downstream agent is permitted to do.

OAuth 2.0 already provides building blocks for expressing delegation. RFC 8693 defines the act claim, which supports nested multi-hop actor identification (enabling a token to express that Agent A delegated to Agent B, which in turn delegated to Agent C). defines the cross-domain transport pattern combining Token Exchange () and JWT Authorization Grant () to carry identity and authorization information across trust domain boundaries. These mechanisms address the runtime side of delegation: who is currently acting, and how to move tokens across domains.
However, two structural gaps remain for agent delegation scenarios:

ul.li: Per-hop authorization constraints: The act claim identifies the actors at each hop but does not record what authorization constraints were applied at each delegation step. A downstream Resource Server sees the final scope but cannot verify whether intermediate agents narrowed or expanded the authorization along the way.

Delegator cryptographic confirmation: The act claim is constructed unilaterally by the Authorization Server. The delegating agent leaves no independent cryptographic evidence that it authorized a specific delegation. This limits non-repudiation and post-hoc audit capabilities.

section.t: This specification introduces the delegation_chain claim as a structured companion to act. While act provides runtime actor identification for authorization decisions, delegation_chain records the full delegation history as an ordered array of delegation records. Each record captures the AS's attestation and the authorization constraints delegated at that hop, and MAY additionally carry the delegator's cryptographic confirmation, so that neither the AS nor any delegating agent can unilaterally construct or deny a delegation record. The two claims coexist in the same token: act identifies the current actor for the Resource Server, and delegation_chain records how the authorization was delegated, step by step, for verification and compliance systems.

The delegation_chain claim addresses delegation lineage and verification, complementing the runtime semantics provided by existing OAuth mechanisms. Cross-domain delegation () addresses the multi-domain scenario. This version of the specification focuses on linear delegation chains; other complex topologies such as diamond-shaped delegation, where multiple paths converge on the same agent, may be addressed by future extensions.

Scope Boundary: This specification addresses problems that lie outside the design scope of Token Exchange () and Identity Chaining (). Token Exchange defines how to convert one token into another but does not record the delegation lineage across multiple hops. Identity Chaining defines how to transport identity across trust domains but intentionally leaves Claims Transcription representation undefined. The two problems addressed by this specification, multi-hop delegation lineage and delegator non-repudiation, are separate from both token conversion and cross-domain transport. Merging this mechanism into either existing specification would broaden its scope beyond its original design intent and impose delegation lineage complexity on deployments that do not need it.

This specification defines the delegation lineage mechanism. The structure of delegated authorization constraints, when carried by reference, is deployment-specific and out of scope of this specification; the consent lifecycle and evidence model belong to separate work.

Relationship to Compositional Approaches: composes existing OAuth mechanisms (Token Exchange, Transaction Tokens, and CIBA) to address agent authentication and authorization. Composition of existing mechanisms alone does not provide per-hop delegator cryptographic confirmation or a verifiable delegation history; that is the layer this specification defines. The two approaches can be used together: compositional frameworks provide the transport and runtime semantics, and delegation_chain provides the structured delegation record and non-repudiation layer.

Relationship to Cross-App Access (ID-JAG): The Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) () profiles Identity Chaining for Cross-App Access (XAA): an application obtains an access token for a third-party API by presenting an identity assertion brokered through the IdP that the downstream Resource Authorization Server already trusts for single sign-on and subject resolution. ID-JAG addresses the identity side of that exchange; its AI agent use case covers a single agent acting as an OAuth client of external tools on behalf of a user. The specification itself marks what it leaves open on the delegation side: it "does not define normative processing requirements for actor_token or whether an act claim is included in the issued ID-JAG", and, beyond requiring that the same ID-JAG not be reused for a different downstream Resource Authorization Server, it leaves propagation across additional downstream hops to "other mechanisms" that "MAY be used", without defining how authorization propagates and narrows along the way.

This specification defines such a mechanism, and the mapping to the gaps above is direct. For the actor delegation that ID-JAG defers to future extensions, this specification defines the delegation record, the delegator's per-hop cryptographic confirmation, and the rules for constructing act when delegation_chain is present (). For the downstream-hop gap, the delegation_chain claim carries the per-hop scope and constraint lineage that a downstream Resource Server verifies (), independently of the IdPs that resolved the subjects at each boundary. For the single-agent use case, the wit:// and spiffe:// agent identifiers () extend the model to agent-to-agent delegation. The two specifications compose at the root authorization: an AS MAY verify the user's identity for the first delegation using an identity assertion grant (), after which delegation_chain records how authorization flowed from that root to the token presenter. ID-JAG resolves who the subject is at a trust boundary; delegation_chain records how the authorization was delegated from that subject.

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

section.title: Relationship to Existing Mechanisms
section.t: This section describes how the delegation_chain claim relates to existing OAuth 2.0 mechanisms, establishing the precise boundary between runtime delegation semantics and structured delegation records.

section.title: Relationship to the act Claim
section.t: RFC 8693 defines the act claim to express that delegation has occurred and to identify the acting party. The act claim supports nested multi-hop actor chains: a token can express that Agent A delegated to Agent B, which delegated to Agent C, all within a single nested JSON structure. This nesting enables Resource Servers to identify the current actor and trace the actor lineage for authorization decisions.

The act claim is constructed by the Authorization Server alone: the AS assembles the nested actor chain without requiring independent proof from each delegating agent. This is sufficient for runtime authorization decisions but does not capture per-hop policy constraints or delegator consent.

The delegation_chain claim complements act by recording the delegation lineage as a structured array of records. Each record captures, when present, the AS's per-hop attestation (as_signature), the authorization constraints applied at that hop (scope, and, when present, delegated_policy_ref), and the delegator's own cryptographic proof (delegator_signature). This enables:

ul.li: Per-hop policy constraints: Each delegation record carries the authorization applied at that hop, not just the final scope. This preserves the full delegation lineage and enables scope narrowing verification.
Delegator proof: The optional delegator_signature on each record provides independent evidence of each delegator's consent, enabling non-repudiation that the AS alone cannot provide.
User interaction: The delegation flow supports optional user consent interaction () at each hop, which is outside the scope of act.

section.t: In a token carrying both claims, act identifies the current actor for the Resource Server's authorization decision, while delegation_chain provides the structured delegation record from the current actor back to the original human principal. The delegatee_id of the most recent delegation record (index 0) MUST match the act.sub value, ensuring continuity between the two claims.

, Section 4.4, expresses multi-hop delegation by nesting act claims within one another, the least recent actor being the most deeply nested. This specification defines a different representation for tokens carrying the delegation_chain claim: in such tokens the act claim contains a single sub value (the current delegatee) and MUST NOT contain a nested act claim. The actor lineage is conveyed by the delegation_chain array instead of nested act claims, so that it is independently verifiable and carries per-hop constraints. Authorization Servers MUST NOT nest act claims in tokens that carry delegation_chain, and Resource Servers MUST NOT expect nested act claims in such tokens. delegation_chain is thus a companion claim that reuses act for current-actor identification while taking over the multi-hop lineage role of nested act claims with a separately verifiable structure.

, Section 4.1, defines the may_act claim, which states that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party. may_act and delegation_chain are complementary: an Authorization Server MAY use may_act in an issued token to pre-authorize specific delegatees for a subsequent delegation hop, and a delegation request naming a delegatee matching may_act is a candidate for the no-interaction path of . The delegation_chain record then captures the hop that may_act enabled. Whether a given delegation is permitted is determined by AS policy, expressed through may_act, a delegation scope, or other deployment-specific means; this specification defines how a permitted delegation is represented and validated.

section.title: Relationship to Identity Chaining
section.t: defines a general-purpose pattern for preserving identity and authorization information across trust domains, combining Token Exchange () and JWT Authorization Grant (). It addresses the transport side of cross-domain delegation: how to move a token from Domain A to Domain B while preserving the user identity and authorization context.
This specification reuses the identity chaining transport for cross-domain delegation () and adds agent-specific extensions:

ul.li: Constraint narrowing enforcement: Each delegation hop carries a scope equal to or narrower than its predecessor; structured constraints (delegated_policy_ref) are attested by the issuing AS when present;

Optional dual-signature security: Both the AS and the delegating agent can sign each delegation record, preventing unilateral forgery; deployments that omit delegator_signature rely on AS signature alone;
Agent Identifier URIs: Resolvable URI-based identity for delegators and delegatees, supporting WIT and SPIFFE schemes.

section.t: The two differ in deployment scope: identity chaining addresses general cross-domain identity propagation (human users, CI/CD pipelines, SSO extension), while this specification profiles that transport specifically for agent-to-agent delegation with delegation lineage requirements.

section.title: Relationship to Claims Transcription
section.t: Section 2.5 of defines Claims Transcription (the process by which Authorization Servers add, change, or remove claims when producing JWT authorization grants or access tokens during cross-domain flows). That specification explicitly leaves the representation of transcribed claims undefined: "The representation of transcribed claims and their format is not defined in this specification."

The delegation_chain claim provides one such representation. When delegation crosses a trust domain boundary, each delegation record captures the transcribed authorization constraints (scope, and when present delegated_policy_ref) and the cryptographic evidence of the transcribing parties (the AS via as_signature and the delegator via delegator_signature, each when present). This enables the receiving domain to verify what was transcribed, who authorized the transcription, and under what constraints, which addresses the representation gap left by identity chaining.

Implementations using identity chaining for cross-domain delegation SHOULD include the delegation_chain claim in the JWT authorization grant as a structured Claims Transcription format, enabling the receiving AS to validate the delegation lineage before issuing a local access token.

section.title: Relationship to Refresh Tokens and Async Refresh
section.t: This specification builds on refresh tokens (); it does not replace them. A refresh token expresses a 1:1 relationship between a client and an Authorization Server: when it is used, the AS re-evaluates and issues a new access token, but the refresh exchange itself carries no record of who authorized what, at which hop, under which constraints. A delegation_chain records exactly that: an N-hop lineage in which each hop carries its own authorization constraints, signatures, and evidence anchor, with scope narrowing propagated along the chain. The two compose: refresh tokens remain the mechanism through which a client obtains fresh access tokens, and the delegation_chain in the issued token preserves the delegation lineage across those refreshes. Concretely, when an Authorization Server issues a new access token in a refresh exchange for a delegated token, it MUST carry the delegation_chain of the refreshed token unchanged: a refresh is not a delegation event and MUST NOT prepend, modify, or drop records.

The asynchronous refresh problem for delegation chains, in which a chained token expires while the user is offline and an agent must refresh it without widening privileges, breaking the identity chain, or impersonating the user, is addressed by Delegated Refresh Tokens for OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (). That specification defines the refresh of delegation chains; this specification defines the chain structure that is being refreshed. The two are complementary and can be combined.

dl.dd: An agent that transfers a subset of its authorization to another agent.
An agent that receives delegated authorization from a delegator.
A single transfer of authorization from one agent to another.
An ordered sequence of delegation hops from the most recent back to the original authorization.
The original authorization granted by a human principal, from which all delegations derive.

A token that cryptographically attests to the identity of a workload or agent, typically issued by a workload identity provider. A WIT URI is a URI that identifies a specific agent and references the WIT bound to that agent's identity.

A URI used to identify a delegating or delegatee agent in a delegation record. This specification defines two URI schemes for agent identifiers: WIT URIs (wit://) and SPIFFE IDs (spiffe://). The identifier MUST be resolvable to a verifiable public key for signature verification when delegator_signature is present.

section.title: Delegation Lifecycle
section.t: A delegation record transitions through four phases during its lifecycle:

ol.li: Delegation Proposal Phase: The delegating agent creates a delegation proposal that includes the delegatee identity, the delegated scope, and, when structured constraints are used, a reference to them and the operation context.

Delegation Interaction Phase (CONDITIONAL): When the Authorization Server determines that user interaction is required before the delegation can be authorized (for example, when delegating to a new agent for the first time, when the delegation involves high-risk operations, or when the delegation crosses trust domain boundaries), the AS returns a delegation_interaction_required response (see ). The delegating agent launches the interaction URI so the user can review and approve the delegation. Upon user approval, the agent retries the delegation request. This phase is skipped when the AS determines that no additional user interaction is needed (e.g., the delegation is covered by a standing authorization or the policy has been pre-approved). Implementations that do not require user interaction MAY omit this phase entirely.

Delegation Enforcement Phase: The Authorization Server validates the delegation request, verifies the delegator's token, confirms that any required user interaction has been completed, verifies the delegator's signature on the delegation_proposal when present, and signs the delegation record upon successful validation. For the first delegation (User to Agent A), the AS MAY additionally verify the user's identity using an identity assertion grant ().
Chain Propagation Phase: The signed delegation record is embedded into an access token's delegation_chain claim, enabling multi-hop propagation within or across trust domains.

section.t: This four-phase model cryptographically binds user authorization, agent identity, and policy constraints at every hop, with explicit user interaction when required.

section.title: Field Definitions

tr.td: A URI identifying the delegating agent. This specification defines two URI schemes: wit:// (WIT URI) and spiffe:// (SPIFFE ID). The URI MUST be resolvable to a verifiable public key for delegator_signature verification.
A URI identifying the receiving agent. The same URI scheme considerations as delegator_id apply.

The delegated scope at this hop, expressed as a space-delimited list of scope values (, Section 3.3). REQUIRED when the chain contains more than one record, so that scope narrowing along the chain is verifiable by any holder of the token; MAY be omitted on single-record chains, where the delegated scope is conveyed by the access token's scope claim. When present, this field captures the scope explicitly authorized at this hop and is included in the signature computation to prevent scope expansion by a compromised AS. The Resource Server verifies that scope narrows monotonically along the chain ().

An opaque reference to the structured authorization constraints that apply to this delegation hop, for deployments that use a structured constraint model. The format and resolution mechanism of the reference are deployment-specific; this specification treats the value as opaque (the same treatment as root_evidence_ref). The referenced constraints MUST NOT expand the delegator's authorization; this is enforced by the Authorization Server at issuance time and attested by the record's signatures. When absent, the delegated constraints are expressed solely by scope.

The SHA-256 hash of the canonical serialization (per ) of the previous (earlier-in-chain) delegation record, i.e., the record at the next higher array index. MUST be present on every record except the earliest (highest-index) record when the chain contains more than one record; MAY be omitted on single-record chains, where there is no earlier record to bind. See for the computation and verification rules.

An opaque identifier referencing the root authorization event (the original consent granted by the human principal from which all delegations in the chain derive). This field MUST be present for the first delegation (User to Agent A) when structured evidence is used and SHOULD be propagated through the chain. The format of the identifier and the mechanism for resolving it are deployment-specific: deployments using a structured authorization evidence model SHOULD set this value to the identifier of the root token's evidence claim; other deployments MAY use any stable, unique identifier (e.g., a consent record ID or an audit log entry reference) that enables post-hoc retrieval of the original authorization context. Implementations not using structured authorization evidence MAY omit this field.

Cryptographic signature from the delegating agent's private key over this delegation record. This provides dual-signature security alongside as_signature, preventing a malicious AS from forging unauthorized delegations and ensuring non-repudiation. Implementations SHOULD include this field on every delegation record. It MAY be omitted when the AS is the sole trust anchor and the deployment does not require independent delegator non-repudiation.

An identifier for the Authorization Server that created this delegation record. This value identifies the issuer of the record's as_signature. In cross-domain chains where records may originate from different Authorization Servers, the as_id enables the Resource Server to select the correct public key for as_signature verification. In single-domain chains, as_id matches the iss claim of the token.

AS signature over this delegation record. When all delegation hops occur within a single trust domain under one Authorization Server, the AS's signature over the issued token already attests to the entire chain and this per-hop signature MAY be omitted. It is RECOMMENDED when delegation crosses trust domain boundaries, so the receiving domain can independently verify each hop.

section.t: The authorization constraints delegated at a hop are expressed as scope: this is the baseline form, REQUIRED whenever the chain contains more than one record so that scope narrowing along the chain is verifiable by any holder of the token. Deployments that use a structured constraint model additionally carry delegated_policy_ref, an opaque reference to the approved constraints. This specification does not define the format, resolution, or comparison of the referenced constraints; narrowing with respect to the delegator's authorization is enforced by the Authorization Server at issuance time () and attested by the record's signatures.
The delegation_timestamp MUST satisfy the following constraints:

ul.li: It MUST be greater than or equal to the delegation_timestamp of the temporally earlier delegation record (the record at the next higher array index), ensuring that timestamps are monotonically non-increasing from index 0 (most recent) to index N (earliest). When the two records were signed by different Authorization Servers (cross-domain chains), this comparison SHOULD tolerate clock skew between the two AS instances, consistent with the freshness window below; a small negative delta between independently clocked hops is not by itself evidence of an invalid chain.

It MUST be within the validity period of the delegator's token at the time of the delegation request (i.e., greater than or equal to the delegator token's iat and less than or equal to the delegator token's exp).

At the time the AS processes the delegation request, the timestamp SHOULD be within an acceptable freshness window relative to the AS's current time. A RECOMMENDED maximum skew is 5 minutes in either direction. Timestamps outside this window SHOULD be rejected to mitigate replay attacks (see ).

section.t: The as_signature and delegator_signature, when present, MUST be computed over the same set of fields. The signature is a JWS () compact serialization. The JWS payload is a JSON object containing exactly the following fields (omitting OPTIONAL fields that are absent); the payload SHOULD be serialized using the JSON Canonicalization Scheme () so that the same set of fields deterministically produces the same bytes across implementations:

ul.li: scope (if present)
delegated_policy_ref (if present)
prev_record_hash (if present)
operation_summary (if present)
root_evidence_ref (if present)

section.t: The prev_record_hash value, when present, is included in the signed field set above. It is computed over the canonical serialization of the earlier-in-chain record: the JSON object consisting of exactly the fields listed above, canonicalized using the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS, ), and hashed with SHA-256. The digest is encoded using base64url without padding (, Section 2). Both signature fields are excluded from the hash input, as they are excluded from their respective signature computations.

Both signature fields MUST be excluded from their respective signature computations. The JWS alg header MUST be set appropriately (e.g., RS256 for AS signatures, ES256 for delegator signatures). The JWS kid header SHOULD be included to facilitate key resolution. The resulting compact JWS string is stored as the value of the respective signature field. When verifying, the verifier decodes the JWS payload and confirms that the decoded JSON object matches the delegation record fields.

When the delegator_signature is present (RECOMMENDED), it uses the delegating agent's agent-identifier-bound private key, while as_signature uses the Authorization Server's signing key. This dual-signature approach, when both signatures are present, ensures:

ul.li: Malicious AS Prevention: A compromised AS cannot unilaterally forge delegations without the delegator's consent;
Non-Repudiation: The delegator cannot deny having authorized the delegation;
Complete Trust Chain: User → AS → Delegator → Delegatee.

section.t: The need for per-hop signatures depends on deployment scope. When all delegation hops occur within a single trust domain under one Authorization Server, the AS's signature over the issued token already attests to the entire delegation chain, and per-hop as_signature and delegator_signature MAY be omitted without loss of integrity. Per-hop signatures become valuable when delegation crosses trust domain boundaries, where the receiving domain must independently verify each hop's authorization, or when non-repudiation from the delegator is required for compliance or audit. This keeps the mechanism lightweight for intra-domain deployments and preserves stronger guarantees for cross-domain agent delegation.

section.title: Key Resolution for Agent Identifiers
section.t: The delegator_signature (and any verification of the delegatee's identity) requires the relying party to resolve the agent identifier to a verifiable public key. The resolution mechanism depends on the URI scheme used in the delegator_id or delegatee_id field:
The wit:// scheme used in the examples of this specification has the following syntax:

The authority component identifies the workload identity provider or trust domain (for example, wit://agent-a.example). The first path segment is the agent identifier, conventionally a digest of the agent's public key prefixed by the hash algorithm, for example, wit://agent-a.example/sha256.aaa111...: once the relying party has resolved the authority to a trusted provider, the identifier itself determines which key material it names. Deployments MAY use other agent identifier forms within the same scheme, provided the deployment documents how the identifier resolves to a key. SPIFFE IDs are used with their usual semantics.

ul.li: wit://: The WIT URI is resolved via the workload identity provider's attestation bundle, which contains or references the agent's public key (e.g., via SPIFFE bundle endpoints);
spiffe://: The SPIFFE ID is resolved via the SPIFFE Bundle Endpoint protocol, which provides the agent's X.509-SVID or JWT-SVID containing the public key.

section.t: Implementations SHOULD document the supported URI schemes and their resolution mechanisms in deployment-specific configuration. If the relying party cannot resolve the agent identifier to a trusted public key, it MUST treat the delegator_signature as unverifiable.

section.title: Chain Ordering and Integrity
section.t: The array MUST be ordered from most recent delegation to earliest:

ul.li: Index 0: Most recent delegation (delegator → current token holder)
Index N: Earliest delegation (first agent after human authorization)

section.t: This ordering allows efficient validation starting from the immediate delegator.

Ordering alone is a syntactic convention; an array of records carries no cryptographic binding between a record and its predecessor. The prev_record_hash field provides that binding. For every record at index i < N in a chain of length N+1, the Resource Server MUST verify that record[i].prev_record_hash equals the SHA-256 hash of the canonical serialization of record[i+1], as defined in (JCS per ). If any prev_record_hash is missing on a multi-record chain, or does not match the computed hash of its predecessor, the chain is invalid and the Resource Server MUST reject the token with an invalid_delegation_chain error.

The per-hop hash binding and the token-level JWT signature provide defense in depth rather than duplicating each other. The token-level signature covers the chain as a whole: any modification, removal, reordering, or splicing of records invalidates it, but it attests only that some AS signed this exact array. The prev_record_hash binding holds independently of the issuing AS's key: because each record's hash is covered by that record's own signatures, a spliced or reordered chain fails hash verification even in scenarios where the token-level signature is not the property in question (e.g., when records from two different chains are combined, or when a chain is re-embedded into a newly issued token by an AS other than the original issuer).

section.title: Ordering Verification Semantics
section.t: The delegation_timestamp and root_evidence_ref fields jointly provide ordering evidence for the delegation chain. This section states explicitly which levels of ordering assurance the mechanism provides, and which it does not.

ol.li: Claim-level ordering: Each record's delegation_timestamp is covered by the record's signatures. Monotonicity across the chain (earlier hops carry earlier timestamps) is verifiable by any holder of the token. This is the baseline property this specification provides.

Cross-party attestation: When per-record signatures are present, each hop's as_signature is produced by an Authorization Server that is independent of the delegating agent at that hop, so the ordering evidence of a hop cannot be forged by the party whose conduct is at issue at that hop. When per-record signatures are omitted (single-domain deployments), this property is carried by the token-level signature of the issuing AS instead. This corresponds to the independently verifiable property discussed for agent action determinability ().

Commit-time enforcement is out of scope: Ordering evidence in the token establishes when delegations were recorded, not that preconditions still held at the time the delegated operation was executed. This specification does not claim commit-time or execution-time atomicity. A fresh observation of a valid chain is not a guarantee that the world has not changed between delegation and execution. Deployments requiring such guarantees MUST combine this mechanism with execution-time mechanisms (e.g., conditional requests, resource versioning) or a commitment or reservation protocol.

section.t: The boundary above is a property, not a mechanism requirement: token-carried evidence records commitments and does not by itself enforce them at execution time. Whatever execution-time mechanism a deployment adds to this specification, the split of responsibilities remains the same: the chain records who delegated what to whom and when; it does not establish that the delegation's preconditions still held at the moment of execution.

section.title: Chain by Reference
section.t: Long delegation chains inflate the size of the JWT access token (see ). For deployments where token size is a constraint, this specification defines the delegation_chain_ref JWT claim: an opaque URI identifying the full delegation chain stored at the issuing Authorization Server. When the delegation_chain_ref claim is present in an access token, the delegation_chain claim is omitted from that token.

The delegation_chain_ref value is opaque to the Resource Server; its resolution mechanism is deployment-specific. A Resource Server typically retrieves the chain via Token Introspection () or a deployment-defined endpoint over TLS. The retrieved representation is a delegation_chain claim value as defined in , and the Resource Server applies the validation rules of to the retrieved chain unchanged. The RS MUST ensure the retrieved chain corresponds to the presented token; when the chain is retrieved through introspection, the response is scoped to the token under validation by itself.

The by-reference form trades the stateless property of JWT access tokens for a smaller payload: the AS MUST retain the stored chain and keep the token introspectable for the lifetime of the token. In particular, an AS that would otherwise issue self-contained JWTs it need not remember MUST NOT issue delegation_chain_ref tokens it cannot later resolve. The delegation_chain_ref value MUST reference a chain retrievable from the AS that issued the token carrying the claim: in cross-domain flows (), that is the receiving AS after chain transcription, not an upstream AS in the original domain, so that the Resource Server only needs a trust relationship with the AS in its own domain.

An AS SHOULD issue the token with delegation_chain_ref instead of the inline delegation_chain claim when the serialized chain exceeds an implementation-defined size threshold. As guidance, chains longer than three records, or whose serialized size approaches typical HTTP header limits, are candidates for the by-reference form. This keeps the token payload constant regardless of chain depth, at the cost of one additional round-trip for chain retrieval and an operational dependency on AS availability at validation time.

section.t: This section defines how a delegation hop is performed with OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (, grant_type=token-exchange): the delegating agent presents its token together with the delegatee's identity and the requested scope, the AS validates the request, and issues a new token for the delegatee carrying the extended delegation_chain. The flow has one branch: when the AS determines that user consent is required for this hop, it responds with a delegation_interaction_required error, the user approves the delegation at the interaction URI, and the agent retries the request; when no consent is required, the AS issues directly ().
